..(Monday night through Saturday)
Issued at 400 AM EDT SUN AUG 30 2026

The most current model data continues to endorse the current 
forecast for a dry and steadily warming period into mid-week with
low to mid 90s on tap for highs at its peak as we get a bit 
hotter each day. We still see the potential for convection in a
good number of the model solutions across forecast area on 
Thursday and Friday - mainly in the afternoon and evening hours
owing to the 5h ridge weakening enough to allow northwest flow to
get close enough that any "ridge riders" can affect our area. Heat 
headlines still may be needed for at least the western parts of 
the area at midweek - still dependent on how effectively higher 
dewpoints can move east into this part of the state. 

The previous long term discussion follows:

Ridging remains the dominant synoptic weather feature at the start 
of the long term forecast period, with the latest guidance 
collectively resolving a 595 decameter ridge directly above the 
commonwealth from Monday to Wednesday. Midlevel heights of this 
magnitude rank above the 99th percentile of model climatology in the 
blended LREF ensemble, and given that such values are the model 
consensus, confidence is high that the Commonwealth of Kentucky will 
experience hot and dry sensible weather conditions this week. The 
ridging should eventually begin to break down by the end of the 
period, but this is marked with a potential transition to more 
active northwesterly flow. Ridge-riding disturbances allow chances 
for showers and storms to reenter the forecast for Thursday, Friday, 
and Saturday, but confidence in the forecast for wet weather at the 
end of the period is lower than it is for hot weather at the 
beginning.

Eastern Kentucky is positioned directly to the east of the mid/upper 
level ridge axis. The related increase in subsidence aloft will 
favor efficient diurnal processes for as long as the pattern 
persists. Expect mostly sunny skies and increasing temperatures 
accordingly, with ridge-valley temperature splits and river valley 
fog emerging at night. Modeled 850mb temperatures climb above the 
20 degree Celsius mark on Monday, remain elevated on Tuesday, and 
then peak closer to 23 degrees Celsius on Wednesday. At the surface, 
this should translate to widespread highs in the lower half of the 
90s on Monday and Tuesday before some locations flirt with the upper 
90s on Wednesday. The warmest temperatures will likely occur in the 
northern half of the forecast area (where heights and 850mb temps 
are the greatest) and in the deepest river valleys (where diurnal 
mixing will be deepest). Blended NBM temperatures are likely too 
warm, and dewpoints likely too moist. As drier air mixes down from 
the midlevels, dewpoints will likely remain below the 70 degree 
line. Heat indices may remain below the 105 degree heat headline 
criteria mark, but it will still feel very hot outside. There won't 
be much relief at night either, with ridge-valley splits above/below 
the 70 degree mark. Interests with outdoor plans (such as high 
school sports, recreational hikes, or camping) are encouraged to 
review heat safety information at weather.gov/safety/heat in the 
coming days. Take frequent breaks in the shade or indoors, stay 
hydrated, and continue to monitor for forecast updates. 

The northeastern periphery of the ridge begins to flatten on 
Thursday, which will allow a NW flow regime to set up over the Ohio 
River Valley. A series of shortwave impulses will then propagate 
around the ridge and towards the forecast area headed into next 
weekend, bringing about the next remarkable chances for showers and 
storms. While 850mb temperatures will trend towards the 20C mark and 
midlevel heights are progged to drop back down towards 590dm by 
then, these disturbances will still be interacting with a seasonably 
warm airmass. Models disagree on the amount of moisture available 
during this pattern shift emerges, but if enough modified tropical 
moisture makes it around the ridge and into the column, this late 
period activity will need to be monitored closely. The available 
machine learning, analog-based, and AI-enhanced long-range 
convective guidance is hinting at more active weather in the Greater 
Appalachians by the end of the period, but it is too early to 
pinpoint specific timing and hazard details. With that being said, 
the clouds and rain-cooled air associated with any convective 
activity would likely mitigate the Major HeatRisk analyzed at the 
beginning of the forecast period. Expect thermometer readings closer 
to climatological norms for the holiday weekend, but monitor for 
updates to the convective forecast while planning any outdoor 
activities for Friday and beyond.
